extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and readers interested in Annie Dillard's life and writing practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted craft principles, procedural choices, and stylistic notes about writing drawn from Annie Dillard's biography and descriptions of her works (e.g., Pilgrim at Tinker Creek, Holy the Firm, Mornings Like This). Useful for writers studying Dillard's methods and creative-writing practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anachronisms in historical fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: While writing The Living, Dillard "never allowed herself to read works that postdated the year she was writing about, nor did she use anachronistic words."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict research and language to period-appropriate sources; deliberately exclude later works and vocabulary that would reveal a later perspective to maintain historical authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found-poetry principle: 'A good trick should look hard and be easy'
rubrics_metrics.description: "A good trick should look hard and be easy," said Dillard about her found-poems book Mornings Like This; the poems were created by taking and arranging phrases from various old books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat found-poetry as craft: the result should appear effortless while hiding labor and careful selection. Aim for an ironic tone and seamlessness so the technique doesn't call undue attention to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-constrained observational writing (micro-period focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Holy the Firm Dillard "decided to begin a project in which she would write about whatever happened on Lummi Island within a three-day time period," and when a plane crashed on the second day she used that event to contemplate pain and natural evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tight temporal constraints (a defined short window) to concentrate observation and detail. A narrow longitudinal focus can yield intense thematic material, but may still require prolonged crafting time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use journals as source material for narrative nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard's journals served as a source for Pilgrim at Tinker Creek.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep detailed journals and mine them for material to preserve immediacy and concrete observation when constructing longer narrative nonfiction pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explore theological/philosophical themes through natural observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilgrim at Tinker Creek "describes God by studying creation," using observation of the natural world to address spiritual questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach abstract or theological issues via concrete natural details and sustained observation rather than merely abstract argument; let nature dramatize philosophical concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdisciplinary reading and active collecting to inform writing
rubrics_metrics.description: As a youth Dillard read widely (geology, natural history, entomology, epidemiology, poetry) and spent time exploring, rock collecting, bug collecting and drawing—activities that "allowed her a way to interact with the present moment."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate curiosity across scientific and artistic disciplines and engage in field observation/collecting to enrich descriptive authority and provide concrete sensory detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from literary predecessors before finding your voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Dillard said, "In college I learned how to learn from other people. As far as I was concerned, writing in college didn't consist of what little Annie had to say, but what Wallace Stevens had to say. I didn't come to college to think my own thoughts, I came to learn what had been thought."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study influential writers deeply to absorb craft and traditions; learning from predecessors is a stage in developing a personal voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Found-text collage method (technique for Mornings Like This)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mornings Like This is dedicated to found poetry: Dillard "took and arranged phrases from various old books, creating poems that are often ironic in tone. The poems are not related to the original books' themes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select phrases from source texts and recontextualize them; accept thematic divergence from originals; use arrangement and juxtaposition to create new meaning and tonal effects (e.g., irony).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an overarching narrative in narrative nonfiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Pilgrim at Tinker Creek contains named chapters, it is not a collection of essays—Dillard constructed it as a coherent nonfiction narrative rather than a loose essay anthology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when using episodic chapters or strong individual pieces, ensure a unifying narrative thread or organizing principle so the work reads as a single cohesive book rather than a disjointed compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short length can demand prolonged, intensive work
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy the Firm was only 66 pages long but "it took her 14 months, writing full-time, to complete the manuscript."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate short page count with little effort; concentrated, compact works often require long gestation and meticulous revision—plan for substantial time investment regardless of final length.
